description_full: Viemed Healthcare, Inc., through its subsidiaries, provides home medical equipment (HME) and post-acute respiratory healthcare services in the United States. The company provides respiratory disease management solutions, including treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which include non-invasive ventilation, percussion vests, and other therapies; and invasive and non-invasive ventilation and related equipment and supplies to patients suffering from COPD. It also sells and rents HME devices, such as non-invasive and invasive ventilators, positive airway pressure (PAP) machines, durable medical equipment, percussion vests, oxygen concentrators, and other medical equipment. In addition, the company provides neuromuscular care and oxygen therapy services; and sleep apnea management which provides sleep solutions and/or equipment, such as PAP, automatic continuous positive airway pressure, and bi-level positive airway pressure machines. Further, it offers in-home sleep apnea testing services; and breast pumps and related lactation equipment and supplies, including fulfillment and support services, as well as healthcare staffing and recruitment services. Viemed Healthcare, Inc. was founded in 2006 and is headquartered in Lafayette, Louisiana.

financial_summary: Viemed Healthcare, Inc. is a small-cap healthcare business with a $346M market cap on $270M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +25% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $12M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -18.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 26× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 14% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
